subsubtopic: FINANCE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS-FOURTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present in both official languages the fourth report of the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs. This report deals with simplification of the Income Tax Act and makes extensive recommendations concerning how Budgets should be prepared and how tax measures should be contemplated so that when presented in a Budget they are drafted simply. It is the view of the committee that simplification of the tax system ought to be a primary concern, while promoting equity and economic growth. The committee has recommended that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay) use a questionnaire type tax reporting form on a trial basis for 1986.
The committee also makes extensive recommendations with respect to how the current Income Tax Act ought to be rewritten to make it readable. You will know, as do others in this House, that it is virtually impossible for Members of Parliament to understand the Income Tax Act. Indeed, senior tax practitioners have indicated they cannot understand the Act themselves. It is with that view that the committee makes this report.

Committee Reports

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: PRICING OF DOMESTIC WHEAT AND ITS PRODUCTS

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Mr. Lome Nystrom (Yorkton-Melville) moves that the first report of the Special Committee on the Pricing of Domestic Wheat and its Products, presented to the House on Thursday, June 5, 1986, be concurred in.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I rise today to move a motion of concurrence in a special report of the House prepared by seven Members of Parliament. It is probably somewhat rare that an opposition Member would move concurrence in a report of a committee on which the Government has a majority. However,
I think the price of wheat in this country is an issue on which we all must agree and one on which we must act quickly if the farmers are going to stay on the land.
While the recommendations of the seven members of the committee were essentially unanimous, of course individual members had some differences. The committee was composed of the Hon. Member for Huron-Bruce (Mr. Cardiff), the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster), the Hon. Member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Gottselig), the Hon. Member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Wilson), the Hon. Member for Gatineau (Mrs. Mailly), the Hon. Member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone) and myself. The committee worked well and it was obvious during our hearings in six different cities that there is a real crisis in agriculture today. The western farmer has not faced such a crisis since the 1930s. In fact, farm income for western Canadian farmers is at approximately the same level as in 1933, in 1933 constant dollars.
I am pleased that the Minister of State for Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) is in the House today. I am calling on him to agree with the recommendations in this report and implement what the Members of three Parties are recommending on behalf of western farmers.
We are faced with a real crisis. The price of wheat is at approximately the 1933 levels, and one can imagine what that means by considering if one's income in another walk of life was at the same level in 1933, in terms of constant dollars. That is why many thousands of farmers are either going bankrupt or facing serious financial difficulties. They will be unable to make ends meet unless we do something.
This special committee was mandated to the narrow study of two-price wheat in this country and to examine, to a very limited extent, the question of parity pricing. I think all of us on the committee realize that we cannot solve the farm problem simply by considering two-price wheat. Two-price wheat represents only 9 per cent of our wheat production in Canada. Another 10 per cent or 11 per cent of wheat production is in feed grains and some 80 per cent of our wheat production is exported to other countries around the world.
I am talking about the problems as they face western Canadian farmers because about 95 per cent of the wheat
produced in Canada is by farmers in the Wheat Board region in western Canada; another 4 per cent is produced in the Province of Ontario; and, the remaining 1 per cent is produced primarily in Quebec, with some in Atlantic Canada. Therefore, this is basically a western Canadian problem.
The solution to that problem is not a domestic wheat price increase. The solution is to bring back some sanity and order to international trade. Presently, there is a tremendous trade war between the Europeans and the Americans, both of whom are massively subsidizing their farmers in the export of grain around the world. We state in our report that the United States is spending some $53 billion American in their agriculture for the next three years in order to subsidize the American grain producers. Some $1 billion of that is being used to subsidize American wheat exports around the world. That $53 billion American is the equivalent of $75 billion Canadian being spent by the United States for subsidies in the next three years, or $25 billion Canadian each year to subsidize the American farmers. How can we compete when the Americans are subsidizing their farmers by some $25 billion Canadian each year?
The U.S. Farm Bill is providing tremendous subsidies for the export of grain. For example, the Americans are selling wheat to Algeria for $104 a tonne, with a subsidy of $54 a tonne. In other words, they are giving one free bushel of wheat for every two bushels they sell to Algeria, as is the case with Morocco. The Americans are after our barley markets in Saudi Arabia and may be after our wheat markets in Syria and other parts of the world. The Americans are fighting against the Europeans, particularly the French, in places like Algeria, Morocco and Egypt. However, if the French are displaced from those markets, the Europeans will go elsewhere and fight for some of our traditional markets.
The real victims of this trade war between the Europeans and the Americans are the Canadian farmers, the Argentinian farmers and Australian farmers. There are only five great grain exporters in the world: Europe, the United States, Australia, Canada and Argentina. That is the current situation.
In addition, as a result of a drop by 19 per cent in world prices for better quality grains, the initial price of wheat went down. The initial price of barley dropped by some 27 per cent this year. Therefore, farm income will decline very rapidly in Canada.
The U.S. loan rate is $2.40 a bushel, which is in effect the price of wheat in the world. We hear much speculation from the Office of Majority Leader Senator Robert Dole and the Office of Mr. Lyng, the U.S. Secretary of Agriculture, that the loan rate in the United States could drop from $2.40 U.S. a bushel to $2.10 U.S. a bushel. The prices would then be lower than those in the 1930s. If that happens and we do not respond, tens of thousands of farmers will go under and we will see the disappearance of many towns and villages and a rural way of life that is so important to this country.
June 19, 1986

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
I believe that all Parties in this House agree that if one segment of our society is in trouble, through no fault of its own, whether it is farmers, fishermen, loggers or anyone else, it is incumbent on the nation as a whole to come to the support of that segment of our society. The farmers in western Canada are in serious trouble, through no fault of their own but because of a trade war, world prices and the increased production of grains in countries like China and India that are becoming increasingly self-sufficient. Consequently, our western Canadian farmers are in trouble.
Some may ask if they could improve their efficiency. As the Hon. Member for Crowfoot, the Chairman of our committee said, the western Canadian farmers is the most efficient farmer in the world with the possible exception of the corn producers in the State of Iowa. Our farmers produce food very cheaply for the people of this country. In fact, we have the second cheapest food in the world in terms of the percentage of our disposable income that is spent on food. We spend about half as much on our food as we did in 1947, which proves that our farmers are not at fault for high prices. Our farmers are very efficient and extremely productive.
Our committee made nine recommendations which I believe should be taken very seriously by the House. I ask the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise), the Minister of State for Canadian Wheat Board and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to accept these recommendations.
The first recommendation is that we retain the present two-price system for wheat. That two-price system has been in place since 1967, when it was brought in to protect consumers. This two-price system meant that when the world price of wheat went high Canadian consumers would not have to pay as much for bread. On the other hand, if the price of wheat in the world was very low, the Canadian price would be somewhat higher so that the farmers would have a better deal and be able to survive on the farm.
What has happened in the 19 years we have had a two-price wheat system? Our committee reports that the consumers have benefited from the two-price wheat system by some $469.5 million because the Canadian price was lower. What about the farmer? On the other side, the two-price wheat system has helped the farmer by only $3.1 million, because only for short periods of time was the Canadian price higher than the world price, so the farmer benefited by $3.1 million and the consumer, when the Canadian price was lower, benefited by some $469 million. Up until now, the two-price wheat system in this country has meant that bread has been lower in price than it might have been; it has meant that the price of Shreddies for everyone in this country has been a little bit lower than it might have been because the farmer, in effect, has helped the consumer keep the price down.
[DOT] (U30)
What we are asking in the report is that the consumer now help the farmer by allowing us to increase the price of wheat from $7 a bushel to $10 a bushel for domestic purposes. With
Committee Reports
an increase of $7 to $10 a bushel, which is an increase of $3 a bushel which will go directly to the farmer, the wheat content will increase by 4.5 cents in a 16 ounce loaf of bread. An increase of 4.5 cents in a 16 ounce loaf of bread is not very much for the consumer to pay to help keep farmers on the land and to ensure that people in my riding, in Swift Current- Maple Creek, and other ridings do not go bankrupt because of the trade war between the United States and Europe.
Wheat for $10 a bushel is only part of the solution, because that concerns only 9 per cent of our production in Canada. However, with such an increase, there would be an extra $220 million in the pockets of western Canadian farmers which would help those farmers in my riding and in other ridings stay on the land. It will help to keep our farm food production system very efficient.
I appeal to the urban consumers represented by urban Members of Parliament in this House by saying that if the farmers are forced off the land and if we have fewer farmers and large corporate farms, the price of food will rise in this country and the people who will suffer in the long run will be the consumers, through an expensive food policy. If the price of food is to be kept down in Canada, we should keep the family farmer operating, and the price of food will be reasonable.
Therefore, I would ask the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer), who is in the House today, to agree to the position we took in committee and increase the price of domestic wheat from $7 a bushel to $10 a bushel.
In my few remaining minutes, I want to mention that recommendation No. 3 is that when export prices improve again the Canadian Wheat Board should review the $10 a bushel wheat price; in other words, if the price of wheat rises internationally from $3 or $3.50 to $5 or $6, we can review the domestic price with a view to dropping it so the consumer will once again get a break in the price of wheat-based products.
To me, recommendation No. 4 is the most important, and that is that the Government should consider a deficiency payment or combination of deficiency payments and stabilization payments for western Canadian farmers. As I said before, domestic wheat is only about 9 per cent of our production. Another 80 per cent is exported; another 10 per cent or 11 per cent goes into feed grains. With the world price of wheat being so low, I believe the farmers of this country must receive a deficiency payment from the federal Government if they are to survive. Our committee, with five Conservative Members of Parliament, unanimously states that the Government should consider a deficiency payment to the farmers of western Canada.
One might ask what the amount should be. In the United States, the farmers are receiving the equivalent of $25 billion Canadian a year. There are more farmers there and it is a bigger economy. However, what the organizations that represent farmers are stating in this country is that the farmers

of Canada should receive $1.5 billion to $2 billion in deficiency payments. I argue that if we can afford to spend, as the Government did last year, $1 billion in bailing out the banks and bank depositors because two banks in Canada collapsed, then surely to goodness we can spend $1.5 billion or $2 billion on a deficiency payment to keep western Canadian farmers in business and on the land. If the farmer is on the land, he or she will be productive, will pay taxes, make a contribution to our society and create jobs.
When the farmer is better off, we are all better off. I know that my friend from Alberta, the Hon. Member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) would agree with that. When the farmers are better off, they will be spending money, creating jobs in the towns and cities of Canada for the young people of Canada. When the farmers get another $2 or $3, they spend $5 or $6. When the farmers spend money they stimulate the economy. It is a Canadian-owned enterprise. The federal Government now must come, on behalf of Canadians as a whole, to the benefit of the farmers, and provide a deficiency payment to ensure that farmers stay on the land. In my opinion, that is the most important recommendation we make in the report.
We also make other recommendations by saying, for example, that we must protect the historical production patterns in terms of wheat production in this country. We must also look at mechanisms to protect our wheat-based industries if the higher domestic wheat price makes them less competitive.
We are also saying, as recommendation No. 7, that the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs should very closely monitor the price of wheat-based products to ensure that there is not undue price escalation, and if the Department identifies unreasonable pricing to the consumer, a public inquiry into the pricing practices of the entire system should be pursued. Many times, the middleman, be it the miller, the processor, the retailer or the wholesaler, will add two or three cents, or five or six cents, or seven or eight cents to the price of a loaf of bread when the price of wheat increases. I maintain that these are unjustifiable price increases. We made a recommendation that the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs closely monitor the price of wheat-based products to ensure that that does not occur.
Another very important recommendation we make is that the Government consider the possibility of a refundable low income tax credit for low income consumers. Bread is a basic staple of life. Low-income people eat lots of bread. If the price of bread increases by 4.5 cents or 5 cents or 6 cents or 7 cents a loaf, then there should be a refundable tax credit so low-income people, even if they do not pay taxes, can file an income tax form and receive a tax credit back from the Government, or $100 or $200 from the Government, whatever we calculate the increase in the price of bread to be for the average low-income family.
Finally, I refer to the ninth recommendation, which is that we lead the way as a country, as one of the five great exporting nations of the world, to ensure that this issue becomes one at
GATT and to make sure that we negotiate a meaningful grains agreement by which the price of wheat will be based on the cost of production so that the farmer will receive his just return and so that consumer nations on the other side will not be charged excessive prices at certain times in the international wheat cycle.
I close by making an appeal to the Government of Canada to accept the recommendations of the committee. Parliament was generous enough to recognize that there was a problem. A committee was struck from all three Parties. Several tens of thousands of dollars were spent in going around this country and studying the situation. We have now made a recommendation, coming from all three Parties, for an increase in the price of domestic wheat from $7 a bushel to $10 a bushel and for a deficiency payment for western Canadian farmers. I appeal to the Minister in charge of the Wheat Board, the Minister of Agriculture and the Prime Minister to accept the recommendations that are made in this report.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have a chance to say a few words on the motion for concurrence in the report on the domestic price of wheat moved by the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom). The committee did a lot of very important work examining the feasibility and benefits of increasing the domestic price of wheat and the impact that would have on agriculture.
At the present time, the domestic price of wheat is about $7. The posted price at Thunder Bay of No. 1 Northern Wheat is something very close to that. However, come July 1 we expect that the international price of wheat will drop. In fact, the initial price posted by the Wheat Board is $3.54. We can see that in the coming crop year, agriculture in western Canada and in the wheat growing areas of eastern Canada is going to face a tremendous drop in income. That was the message we heard most strongly in the West as well as throughout the country.
Agriculture is facing the most serious challenge it has faced since the 1930s. In fact, the price of wheat that we expect in the coming crop year will in real dollars approach the level it was in 1933. It was very appropriate therefore that this committee examine the question of a domestic price of wheat.
A domestic wheat-pricing mechanism has been used throughout the years to provide subsidies to consumers, amounting to something like $469 million. Very little of that has gone to the farmers. Perhaps something in the order of $2 million or $3 million has gone to the farmers, and that information is all contained in the report.
The key issue is that the downturn we will see in wheat prices, as posted by the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer), of 20 per cent in gross revenues will have a devastating effect on the agricultural community. 1 do not think anyone can really appreciate how devastating it will be. If the commodity price goes down by 20 per cent, land values will probably go down by 10 per cent. A young farmer who is highly leveraged will not only see his income decrease, but will see his equity decrease as well. The situation is very grim.
I suppose the most distressing part of the situation for Canadian wheat growers is that American commodity producers are receiving deficiency payments which lift their prices from something like $3.50 to about $6.10 per bushel. The European Economic Community farmers in France, Germany and the U.K. are benefiting from similar kinds of support programs. The impact of the world downturn in wheat prices will not be felt as much by them as it will be by Canadian farmers. In fact, one analysis in a Chase Econometrics study which I read suggests that net farm incomes will drop as much as 20 per cent this year across the entire country. We are facing a very difficult problem.
I was quite pleased to note that in eastern cities, most consumer and retail groups seem to be very conscious of what is happening in Canada, particularly to western grain farmers who produce 96 per cent of the wheat, as well as other wheat growers in eastern Canada. These groups seem to be sympathetic to and concerned about this problem.
Let me refer to a couple of recommendations made in the report. One is that Canada continue to pursue in a very active way having agriculture commodity pricing and marketing put on the agenda at the general agreement on tariffs and trade
June 19, 1986

meeting which will be held in Uruguay this fall. Unfortunately, when the Group of 7 heads of Government met in Japan, wheat was not one of the commodities recommended to go to GATT. The seven leaders talked about services, foreign investment and intellectual rights being referred to GATT for negotiation, but bringing farm commodity prices under the general provisions of the GATT arrangement was not recommended. I was pleased to have read a press report yesterday indicating that the European Economic Community is pressing for agriculture commodities to be brought under the GATT.
The committee also heard a lot of testimony indicating that profit levels in the milling industry in particular are very high. We were not able to substantiate that, but a report that was often referred to by witnesses indicated that the profit levels in the milling industry in Canada approached $21 per tonne compared to some $3.50 per tonne in the United States. The committee was concerned about, but was not able to authenticate that charge. It recommended in the report that the Consumer and Corporate Affairs Department do a careful investigation of the milling industry and, if indications of price gouging are found, that a full public inquiry be established by the Government to look into that, and supposedly take action in that regard.
The committee enumerated two solutions for dealing with the farm income problem. One was to increase the domestic price of wheat from $7 to $10. If the Government decides to do that, it will generate some $220 million worth of benefits for farmers. Unfortunately, the total impact on Canadians could be as high as $675 million, because in some sectors the value added is not 100 per cent but is up to 200 per cent. If the domestic price of wheat is increased by $3 per bushel, a 24-ounce loaf of bread will contain 6.5 cents more wheat, but the consumer price will be 13.5 cents higher per loaf. In other commodities the increase would triple rather than double.
Increasing the domestic price of wheat will generate approximately $220 million for Canadian agriculture, but at the same time we will have to pay almost twice that to the millers, the bakers, the distributors and the retail stores. In fact, some groups indicated that when the price of domestic wheat rose by only $1 back in the early spring, it should have resulted in an increase of about 2.2 cents per 24-ounce loaf of bread. Additional costs in the price of grain would double that to around 4.5 cents. In some markets, such as those of the corner stores or smaller towns which do not have the highly competitive situation that exists in supermarkets, the increase was actually in the order of 10 cents or almost double what we were generally told would be the market activity. Although we found that the increase for a 24-ounce loaf was 13.5 cents, in many markets it could have been much higher than that. That solution is one solution, but I personally favour a direct deficiency payment, about which I will talk later this morning.
The repercussions or resulting impacts of the domestic price increase are almost as worrisome as the fact that farmers only
Committee Reports
receive about a third of the additional costs, while the millers, bakers, and distributors receive two-thirds. If we increase the domestic price by $3, in order to protect our baking industry we would have to provide tariff protection. In many markets we would see wheat-based products flowing into Canada, and I assume we would have to provide tariff protection of at least 13 per cent, 15 per cent, or 20 per cent. At a time when the Government is attempting to negotiate a free trade agreement,
I just cannot imagine that it would want to impose a tariff on wheat-based products coming into Canada. However, if the Government does not do that, certainly the pasta industry, the bread industry, and many other baked products industries will have a very difficult time, because the projections for wheat prices this year indicate a possible $6 per bushel difference. If the world price goes down by approximately $4, and our domestic price is $10, we will be looking at a $6 differential and obviously a tariff would be required.
The committee made another recommendation which it thought would be necessary if the domestic price were increased by $3 per bushel. It recommended a refundable tax credit for low-income families. The committee staff has estimated that to cost about $115 million. Therefore, it equals more than half the value which farmers would realize from the $3 increase. That detracts from the desirability of the $3 per bushel increase.
Another concern registered by the committee was that if we increased the domestic price by $3, we would have a drastic change in marketing and production. We have already seen some change this year. For example, last year Ontario produced some 220,000 bushels of hard spring wheat, and this year the projection is that it will be 3 million bushels. Likewise, soft winter wheats have been traditionally produced in Ontario. I am sure southern Alberta, which produces about 33 per cent, would look with great desire upon producing more soft winter wheats because of the differential in price that may go as high as $6 per bushel. I think the committee recognized that, and that if the Government were to use this mechanism it would have to put in place some method of market controls so there would not be drastic distortions.
Also the committee recommended that this should be a short-term proposition. Let us look at the world situation. If the world market price rises, we should lower the domestic price once farmers are receiving an adequate return on their cost of production.
The recommendation which I favour is one that has less repercussion; that is, to move to a straight deficiency payment. The Liberal caucus and the Liberal Party have recommended a payment of some $30 per tonne to reinstate, essentially, the 1985-86 crop year initial prices. We estimated that on the wheat portion this would cost $660 million. I think that amount reconciles with the $750 million or $800 million figures discussed in committee which would be required to reestablish 1985-86 initial prices for western grain. Of course, consumers will pay. If the world price drops to $4, there will be a $3 advantage for which consumers will pay.

June 19, 1986
Introduction of Bills
When we look at the prospect of a $3 increase, which delivers only $220 million to farmers, it seems to me that a straight deficiency payment would provide three times that amount or some $660 million. That would be much more adequate for wheat production. We would not have to get into the problem of imposing tariffs. We would not have to get into the problems of production and marketing controls among various wheat producing portions of the country. We would not have to get into the question of a refundable tax credit. We would not have to worry about rebates being provided by the Canadian Wheat Board to wheat-based product manufacturers who market their products in the United States. All in all, we would put in place a fairer system, because it would be distributed to all producers, not just those in the No. 1 and No. 2 wheat pools, as would be the case with a strict benefit through the domestic wheat price system.
I hope the Minister of State for Canadian Wheat Board will be able to announce today a deficiency payment of adequate size. I recommend to him that it be at least $30 per tonne, based upon No. 1 wheat. At least we would then come to grips, in an initial way, with the kind of Herculean demand or problem facing the Canadian wheat producing industry which will have a devastating impact upon western agriculture, especially in this coming year. There will be a smaller impact upon wheat producers in eastern Canada as well. However, since 96 per cent of wheat production is in the West, the impact of the anticipated low prices will be very serious. I hope the Minister will be able to make that announcement today or in the very near future, because we are only five weeks or six away from the start of the new crop year.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a brief comment and then ask a question of the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster). I personally want to commend him for his excellent work on the Special Committee on the Pricing of Domestic Wheat. I was pleased to note that he correctly identified and elaborated on the problems faced by Canadian agriculture and the difficulties in which the Canadian farmer finds himself.
I am concerned though that the Hon. Member dissented to the report which was agreed upon by the rest of the committee. He called for a straight deficiency payment as the sole answer. If I understand the Member correctly, he feels the Canadian consumer, despite the history of the two price wheat system, ought not to shoulder at least some of the burden through perhaps a modest price increase in wheat-based products. The Hon. Member suggests that the answer to this and presumably all other problems is for Government as always to raid the treasury, to borrow more money, to increase the national debt and the interest charges that go with it. Yet this policy and attitude has clearly placed Canada and Canadians in a rather severe economic situation.
I heard earlier the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) state that the benefit of the proposed increase in the domestic wheat price from $7 to $10 a bushel would be something in the order $220 million to Canadian wheat producers. I ask the Hon. Member for Algoma to remember that, according to records of Agriculture Canada and Statistics Canada, the total farm debt outstanding in 1984 was something in the order of $21 billion. A 1 per cent increase in interest rates then could manifest itself in a $210 million additional expense to Canadian agriculture by way of interest costs. Similarly, if deficit reduction measures are successful and lower interest rates result, then there could be a resulting decrease in interest costs. That is surely what responsible deficit reduction measures should be trying to attain.
I know the Hon. Member's concern for agriculture and I know that he would not want to see the Government get into a Catch-22 situation where by rushing forward with payments out of the treasury we would compound the problem by increasing the national debt, and increasing interest costs. This would put upward pressure on interest rates, which in turn would cause the farmers more grief than they already have. I know that calling for a straight deficiency or a stabilization payment has appeal. It is awfully easy and it is simple, but I suggest to Hon. Members that it is also very seductive and
June 19, 1986

highly dangerous. I suggest to the Hon. Member for Algoma, considering the problem and the history of the two-price wheat system, which has helped the consumer in the past, that perhaps now in this time of difficulty for Canadian wheat producers turnabout is fair play and the consumer should bear some part in the solution to this problem. It may well be that the situation will call for deficiency payments as recommended by the committee. Surely the Hon. Member cannot expect the treasury to bear the entire burden of this and every other problem facing our society. Would he elaborate on that please, Mr. Speaker?

Mr. Speaker, it occurs to me that if the domestic price of wheat is maintained at $7, as I would suggest, and the world price drops to $4, consumers will be paying some $220 million in the months ahead-if those projections occur. The net benefit of the $3 increase is $220 million whereas the actual over-all cost to the country is up to $675 million and there is a disproportionate benefit to the millers, bakers, distributors and retailers. On top of that, Mr. Speaker, there is a benefit of $220 million to the farmers, yet at the same time the Government is putting in place a low income refundable tax credit that will cost $115 million, which is more than half of the benefit to the farmers, plus all these other problems of putting in place a tariff and production and marketing controls. As a result, the net benefit to the farmer is low, yet you create all these distortions.
It seems that what we want to do is to deliver in the most efficient way possible as many dollars as possible to the farmer. By raising the domestic price of wheat is one way, and maybe the Government will decide to do it that way. The amount of money paid out to manufacturers, distributors and retailers together, along with the low-income refundable tax credit, will cost something like $785 million, yet the farmer gets only $220 million. That does not seem like a very efficient way to me.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Kelleher) I assume have to look at the repercussions of imposing a tariff. You do not put on tariffs like that in a minute, but you would have to so to protect the bakery manufacturers. In places like Vancouver, the Washington State manufacturers already have 20 per cent of the market. The pasta people say they will be wiped out because everybody will be shipping Durum wheat to Italy where it will be processed. The European Economic Community will put on variable levies and then there will be the reconciliation benefits as the pasta comes back out. This does not seem to me to be very efficient, when we are trying to provide a substantial benefit to farmers.
I think there was general agreement in the committee that we need to provide a substantial benefit to the farmers. If we go the domestic price increase route then we have a very substantial cost. It provides only about one-third of what is generally discussed as being needed as a basic deficiency payment, and then you have to provide a deficiency payment as well. The distortions and the net benefit to the farmer are so

low compared to the straight deficiency payment that it does not seem to me to be a good thing.

were here for this debate. Although not as spectacular as question period, which will start at two o'clock, the subject of this debate has a far greater impact and is far more important to them personally than the proceedings that will start at two o'clock this afternoon.
That is because, Mr. Speaker, this report and the work done by the committee that examined the pricing of domestic wheat, are a perfect example of the principles that should guide this Parliament, our Government and all Members of this House. I am referring to the co-operation and support one part of the country should show another that is experiencing a crisis.
It is true that wheat is consumed across this country, Mr. Speaker, but it is produced, it is mainly grown in Western Canada, and to a lesser extent in Ontario, while less than 1 per cent of our wheat is grown in the other provinces, including Quebec. Mr. Speaker, our wheat growers are in trouble, but the problems they are facing are not of their own making. It is not because wheat growers in Western Canada are not productive enough or made the wrong decisions or did not work hard enough or were not smart enough to cope with and prevent the crisis they are facing today.
No, it is because the world price paid for their wheat has dropped dramatically and probably will drop even more until it reaches a level where they can no longer continue their operations and make a profit as well.
Our special committee, on which I sat as vice-chairman, made its recommendations in this report with a view to protecting Canada's rural economy and our agri-food industry. Although most of our wheat is grown in the West, it is sold to the processors who are located in Central and Eastern Canada. In other words, Mr. Speaker, the jobs in the agri-food industry are in the latter two areas.
Therefore, the purpose of today's debate is to explain to our colleagues in the House and to our fellow citizens that, when examining the pricing of domestic wheat, the special committee was also concerned about the agri-food industry and the consumer. And that, as was explained by the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster), is because any increase in the domestic price of wheat automatically increases the price of products that contain wheat.
It was our duty to ensure that any solution we proposed to deal with the wheat grower's problems would not harm our agri-food industry, our processors, our manufacturers of wheat-based products and especially the consumer, and there again, especially those Canadians on low incomes who are far more dependent on such products. I am thinking for instance of the various kinds of pasta that make up a large part of the diet of those Canadians who unfortunately are not as well off as many of us in this country.
The challenge to be met by our committee was: to provide an emergency solution for a whole industry that is mainly concentrated in one part of this country, while protecting another industry that is mainly located in another part of the country.
In our report we have tried to deal with this problem. We had to use a mechanism that was already in place, since we did not have time to set up other mechanisms that, as the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) said, and rightly so, might have resolved the problem on an ad hoc basis, without the need for setting up all kinds of controls and monitoring agencies and quota systems to cope with any over-reaction from processors who will have to absorb any increases in the production price and the price of the primary ingredient of their food products.
The existing mechanism was the double price system for wheat, including a domestic price, which the Government of Canada has been able to control over a number of decades. The system has been in existence since 1967, Mr. Speaker. Initially, it was aimed at helping producers who were faced with prices that were far too low on the international market. The two-price system for wheat was also developed and maintained, to help consumers and prevent major increases in the prices of certain food products, such as bread, pasta and other wheat-based products.

This is why, after making an in-depth assessment of the need to retain this two-price system to ensure the survival of wheat producers, especially in Western Canada, but also in part of Ontario, the members of the Committee did decide to maintain this system because it could be used immediately for the 1986-87 crop year which will begin on August 1 in Western Canada.
Second, we were well aware of the fact that the crisis facing Western wheat producers is the result of external factors, namely the enormous subsidies which farmers in Common Market countries in Europe receive from their Governments to sell their wheat at a more than competitive price, which creates inequities on the world market.
The United States, which are also major wheat producers, reacted by introducing a protectionist bill to keep up with the enormous subsidies which exist in Common Market producing countries.
Our wheat exports have given us in the past a standard of living which would not have been possible in Western Canada, or indeed in other regions, but unfortunately, our country relies a lot on exports, much more than other producing countries. We are therefore facing a crisis because our producers rely on the world market to purchase 80 per cent of their production.
As for the remaining 20 per cent, Mr. Speaker, 10 per cent are for human consumption and it is this part of the production that we have had to examine.
When we look at the recommendations contained in this report, we find that it recommends an increase from $7 to $10 a bushel in the domestic price of wheat. What is really unfortunate, Mr. Speaker, is that the $3 a bushel increase will bring only about $180 million at the most, of relief to the
June 19, 1986

wheat producers for whom the crisis means a shortfall in their income of maybe $700 million compared with last year.
The initial price of wheat announced by the the Canadian Wheat Board will mean a shortfall of this magnitude for wheat producers. In our opinion, if we were to avoid causing too much upheaval in the agro-food industry and hitting the consumers too hard, and if we wanted to add controls and safeguards for the consumers, such as when we ask for the assistance of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs or suggest a tax credit for the disadvantaged, the maximum increase permissible would bring up the price to $10.
Accordingly, where do we get the difference in losses between the $180 million at the most that can be derived from a serious and responsible increase, and the $700-odd million needed to have them back in a situation similar to that of last year? This is why we also recommended that an extra payment be added to the increase in the price of domestic wheat.
Earlier, my colleague for Algoma (Mr. Foster), in answer to my questions in which I suggested that if we had covered that loss of revenue simply by an added payment, without changing the domestic price for wheat, replied that perhaps hundreds of millions would have to be found. But, finally, could he explain where those hundreds of millions would come from, which would have to be added up to the national debt... Could we over-burden the agro-food industry or the farming industry with an increased interest charge that would result from increasing the deficit in order to allow a full added payment without changing the domestic wheat price? We would not know where those additional funds would come from and they could as well be attributed he said ... for instance, to the expenditures incurred by the Prime Minister's Office. I would suggest to him, Mr. Speaker, that the Prime Minister's Office can only spend within the budget that was approved in the Estimates, and this has nothing to do with the national debt. Moreover, he referred to the western banks which were in difficulty and which the Government chose to help because their depositors were in a critical situation. He said that if the Government had $1 billion to spend helping the Banks, why would it not have $1 billion to help wheat producers?
That argument does not hold, Mr. Speaker, because the Government did not help those banks. What the Government did, and indeed it was a critical situation, it helped depositors, small municipalities, people with small savings, even unions, farmers' unions, even farmers. My colleague for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) gave instances of farmers in his constituency, in his municipality, where everybody would have lost $50 because of the debt the municipality would have been left with had not the Government of Canada helped those depositors. It is therefore twisted logic to suggest that the Government is able to find funds when it wants to. This is not the way things work. And, anyway, perhaps it is because of the approach to the national debt which the previous administration had, and which was supported by the Hon. Member for Algoma that at one time we found ourselves with those interest rates between
Committee Reports
22 and 25 per cent that sent our western wheat producers belly-up and which may have sent farmers in his own Ontario constituency belly-up too. Because whenever interest rates increase by one point under the pressure of a growing deficit, an extra $210 million must be paid by wheat producers. And as we very well know for those producers, especially the younger ones with the most productive farms, loans are absolutely essential to remain on top of things, to get the equipment needed for large farms to remain viable, and 22 per cent interest rates are an unacceptable burden to anyone. Not only to wheat producers or farmers generally, but also to homeowners. Just how many of them have lost their properties when interest rates were sky-high during the 1982 crisis?
Mr. Speaker, having considered all these challenges and problems, the Committee has come up with the recommendations which appear in its report.
I, for one, believed that it was really an emergency response to recommend a price increase for wheat from $7 to $10 a bushel. I was personally quite concerned about the consumers, especially the least affluent of them, having to assume an excessive increase. That is why we have this recommendation that the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs be empowered to control the increase passed on to consumers.
It is for that reason also, Mr. Speaker, that, as indicated in the Minutes of Proceedings, it was I who moved a motion that the two price wheat policy be temporarily maintained and that it be used to help producers in a crisis situation. However, I had suggested a more modest increase.
Mr. Speaker, in a democratic system, the voice of the majority should prevail whether we agree or not with a proposal. That is why I find that, generally speaking, this report, with its control measures, the monitoring power granted to the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, a recommendation to the Government of the day to negotiate a better treaty to support the world price for wheat and make our producers more competitive-was a responsible approach.
That is why I have accepted that my motion calling for a price increase to $8 on January 1, and to $9 next August, be defeated. Mr. Speaker, I have been persuaded that wheat producers needed these $180 million right away, at the end of crop year 1986-87, and that thanks to our monitoring and control measures, we could effectively protect consumers.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I would like to suggest that the Government of Canada, my Government, might seriously consider a proposition I made: instead of increasing domestic wheat prices it should impose a business transfer tax on the entire wheat processing industry and set these funds aside for the agri-food sector. This would make it possible to help producers through critical periods, and consumers would pay only for the portion going to the producers.
These are my closing words, Mr. Speaker. I strongly urge the Government to give serious consideration to this mechanism I am proposing, for I think it would be widely accepted

June 19, 1986
Committee Reports
by consumers and their associations. I think we should review the two-price system for wheat because, very useful though it may have been in the past, it is no longer adequate to cope with the kind of crises we can expect as a result of all these world market fluctuations.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to comment on this. Yes, it was a rather imaginative suggestion from our colleague.

As my colleague from Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Wilson) knows there were a few drawbacks to the suggestions made by our colleague. One of them was that the emergency was staring us in the face. We had to have some help for our wheat producers for the 1st of August. The tariff or tax that our colleague was suggesting, although it did have some equity features and various other aspects which would have solved a lot of the problems, could not be put in place immediately.
Therefore, it was very difficult for us to want to rely on such a recommendation when we did not know exactly how this mechanism was going to work. That was one of the drawbacks.
A second drawback was the fact that it would be a tax on food. We do not have a tax on food in this country, and there is something a little abhorrent about taxing food. We find that having to pay a tax when we go to a restaurant is not very pleasing, but to put it on food, and particularly on bread and pasta, which is consumed in the major part by the poorer people in our society, was something we were uneasy with.
There was also a third drawback, and that was when we consulted some of the Finance Department officials about it. They pointed out to us the difficulty of implementing such a tax or a tariff because of the fact that it would be based on the wheat content in the products. There would not be a tax on the
wheat itself, it would be on the product that was derived from the wheat. Therefore, how would you define which product would be taxed and which product would not? That was one problem.
Another problem was that it would be at the retail level. Since bread is sold in hundreds and hundreds of small stores, the idea of every one of these little family corner stores having to amend and modify its cash register in order to have to collect this tax on some items, and maybe not on others, presented some difficulties.
It did have advantages. As a matter of fact, in our report we mention that we realize that using the domestic price of wheat to help the wheat producers was an emergency situation, and we should look at other ways of generating some funds so that we can help producers when they are in a crisis situation.
One of the things that was suggested was that we look at various mechanisms which would permit the raising of funds from the middle people, the manufacturers, and make sure that, whatever the price of wheat is, the benefits of any increase that would go towards the price of wheat would be given to the producer.
Therefore, I think that if the Government of Canada accepts our report it will be looking at the mechanism that was suggested by our colleague and would then be able to see whether we can overcome the drawbacks that I have mentioned.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak on this concurrence motion. The committee faced a difficult task in looking into the problems of the two-price system for domestic wheat. It became obvious that the question of increasing the price of domestic wheat was more complex than originally thought and needed to be considered very carefully.
While it is the Government's responsibility to decide whether it will accept these recommendations, particularly the two-price recommendation of $10 per bushel for domestic wheat, it should recognize a number of valuable points raised in the report.
First, the report may have increased the awareness of other parts of Canada, other than the wheat-producing areas of the Prairies and Ontario, about the problem facing grain producers and the need for more cash flow in farming generally.
The recommendation of $10 per bushel was clearly recognized as not being a solution, but simply a means of adding a little extra to the coffers of the wheat producers.
Since this recommendation somewhat ignores the total problem of cash flow, the committee went on to suggest that while this may help, there will still be a deficiency for grain producers as far as cash flow is concerned.
Since we use only some 10 per cent of the wheat we produce, this recommendation would add some 35 per cent to the price
June 19, 1986

of perhaps 1 or 2 per cent of the total grain produced. This does not represent a bail-out of farmers across the country.
The report also recommends deficiency payments for grain producers which may ultimately be the most effective and worth-while of all the recommendations. The report recognizes the effect that increasing the price of domestic wheat may have on low income consumers and suggests that the Government should protect them from large increases, if it accepts the recommendation.
The report also warned against the danger of increasing the cost of wheat products which may have to compete against imported products and recommended that the Government ensure that this did not happen.
It is obvious that the committee did a very thorough job in not only looking at the problem of cash flow, which was its particular mandate, but looking at other problems which arose as part of the whole approach.
The greatest value of this report, apart from its recommendations which are now before the Government, is possibly the fact that it will make the rest of the country aware of the need to do something about the cash flow of grain producers so they may continue to operate even with the current low price for grain?
The Government will have to consider several alternatives to inceasing the domestic price of wheat. One of the alternatives suggested in the report is deficiency payments. Some action has already been taken with respect to the cost of production, an area in which the Government can possibly do more if it decides to increase domestic payments. The Government has taken steps with respect to the price of farm fuel and has removed the federal tax on both diesel and regular fuel to the point where the tax is only a fraction of a cent per litre. Fertilizer is a major cost to wheat farmers, and while its price has decreased somewhat, it is only because the farmers have not bought as much fertilizer. The price of fertilizer has not even been affected by the reduction in the world price of oil. This is an area in which the Government could take action.
The Government has not taken steps to reduce the input costs to farmers, such as the cost of chemicals, and therefore reduce the requirement for large deficiency payments. If the cost of production can be reduced by a few dollars per acre, the requirement for bringing deficiency payments up to the cost of production will not be so great.
I hope the Government is prepared to produce its debt review structure for which we have been waiting. Such a mechanism would not particularly increase the income of farmers, but it would help them to remain in business. We hope this debt review structure will have the authority to force creditors to recognize that there is a problem and farmers must be given the opportunity to recuperate from the disasters of the low price of grain.
The farmers are carrying a $28 billion debt and, much like the situation faced by the Government, much of their cash
Committee Reports
flow is used to service the interest on that $28 billion debt. Maybe that is a good place for the Government to start. Maybe we should be eliminating, as far as possible during these times of low commodities, the cost of servicing that debt.
The Government has also taken some action, at least, in freezing the cost of transportation, which has become another major factor over the last few years, in delivering grain to the world market. But most of all, I suppose what the Government must do, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) expressed it a few weeks ago, is to try to break the cycle of subsidies that are being paid in other countries and to put the structure of the sale of farm products, particularly grain, much closer to the cost of production level than is presently happening, with the U.S. and the European Common Market subsidizing as much as 70 per cent of the cost of production.
I must also express my concern that the Government has not consistently placed before the agricultural community a policy which indicates that it is really serious about making it possible for the farmers to stay on their farms. In fact, just last week, the Deputy Minister suggested that the main policy approach of the Government of Canada must be the elimination-although I am sure he did not use that word-of 20 per cent of the farmers during the next few years, and to help ease the pain of getting those farmers off the land. It would be interesting to know if this is the basic policy that the Government is accepting, that it has moved away from the protection of the family farm and is now finding methods of getting 20 per cent or more of the farmers off the land, into the transition program and, consequently, no longer producing. However, I would point out to the Government in this case that, farmers being what they are, eliminating a certain portion of the farmers from the structure will not solve the problem, because the farmers who take over the land will produce grain on the same land and if they cannot receive cost of production, they will not survive very long. We will still be facing exactly the same problem as we do now in the pricing of grain.
As in the past, we again call on the Government, even as it considers these recommendations and makes decisions as to how they will be implemented,to take a global look at agriculture and the possibility of establishing some kind of parity pricing, which would mean that in all of the agricultural areas, all of the commodity producers could look forward to a price which would at least give them the cost of production. In cases of emergency, that cost of production does not need to be much higher than exactly the basis of the input plus the cost of the land, in some kind of a capacity so that a large portion of the farmers can survive.
The Farm Credit Corporation told us just yesterday that it feels that 22 per cent of farmers across the country are in some kind of financial difficulty and that as many as 6,000 people to whom it has lent money are no longer able to make any payments on their debt and that 2,000 of them are beyond saving. That situation is growing. If it is that bad now, it will

June 19, 1986
Committee Reports
be worse by the fall. In the grain-producing part of the country, with prices going down on August 1, we can expect a fairly major increase in the percentage of farmers who will be looking someplace else to make a living.
Although I am not wildly supportive of increasing the price of domestic wheat to $10,1 think that if it is the only direction we can go, then we must accept it, with all the problems that are there; but there are other ways of doing it, and I hope that the Government will look at them. The main one, also a recommendation of the committee, is that the Government recognize the need for deficiency payments to increase the cash flow. There should be recognition that a very small portion of our total grain production would be affected by increasing the domestic price of wheat and, consequently, going through the process of protecting the low-income consumer and ensuring that our wheat products are still competitive in the world against the exports that we will have to face, may make it much easier for the Government to say, "Let us establish a deficiency payment level, put that in place, and not worry about the domestic price of wheat". In the process, not only would the wheat producers be helped a little bit, but it would help all grain producers quite a lot. That would be a solution recognized by the committee, but it would not have the real, inherent problems with which the Government would have to deal if it were to accept the recommendation of two-price wheat or the domestic wheat price at $10 a bushel.
I hope that the Government takes a good look at the report and then recognizes that there are other ways of dealing with the problem, ways which are less difficult and more likely to solve the numerous problems faced by farmers, not only those in the grain area, but also those involving most of the commodities that are today much lower in price than the cost of production.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to join in this debate concerning the report of the Special Committee on the Pricing of Domestic Wheat and Its Products. This is a committee which was formed as a result of a Private Member's Motion moved on December 13 of last year to the effect that a committee be appointed to prepare and bring in a Bill with the objective of providing higher returns for wheat producers from wheat sales for human consumption in the domestic market-place while avoiding undue hardship to processors, consumers and other wheat users.
In moving such a motion last December I made reference to the farm income crisis facing Saskatchewan and Canadian agriculture, with particular reference to the grain farmer. Some 80 per cent of the Canadian wheat crop is marketed internationally, which accounts for much of Canada's favourable balance of trade in agriculture. The remaining 20 per cent of Canadian production is used domestically, with approximately half of it going toward animal feed and the other half finding its way into wheat-based products for human consumption. Unfortunately, record world wheat crops have increased
June 19, 1986

carry-over stocks, depressed prices and lowered expected volume. I would like to give some background with particular reference to my Province of Saskatchewan where there are some 66,000 farmers.
The average farm size is about 1,000 acres. The average capital investment is $480 per acre. In 1984 the average net income per farm was $15,000. For the year 1985, according to figures provided by the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, after deducting operating expenses and depreciation, the average realized net income for each one of those farms was something in the order of $5,500. From that sum of $5,500 the farm family has to find room to make payments on the principal on loans, to meet all of its other expenses, including living expenses, food, clothing, utilities and so on. This sum of $5,500 represents the farmer's labour, as well as his return on a capital investment of some $500,000. Since those comments were put forward last December, the situation has deteriorated considerably.
The initial price of wheat announced for the forthcoming crop year, 1986-87, which commences August 1, is 81 cents per bushel less than last year. It was against that backdrop that the Special Committee on the Pricing of Domestic Wheat and Its Products was finally formed in the month of March, with a mandate to conduct hearings on the domestic wheat price and also on parity pricing.
The committee was heartened, I believe, by the announcement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) that the range under which domestic wheat would be priced would be increased from the existing $5 to $7 range per bushel to a range of between a minimum of $6 and a maximum of $11 per bushel. In doing this I believe that the Prime Minister signalled to wheat producers and to committee members that he was prepared to take a serious look at the domestic wheat pricing situation. The seven-member committee heard representations and received presentations from interested groups representing all of the players: the consumers, the processors and the wheat growers. These hearings were conducted in cities across the country and here in Ottawa.
Basically, three alternatives presented themselves to the committee. The first was simply to maintain the current domestic wheat price of $7 per bushel. I believe that that was found to be unacceptable because Canadian wheat producers, while perhaps being the most efficient in the world, cannot fight the combined treasuries of western Europe and the United States which are subsidizing their producers to the hilt.
It is not accpetable to suggest that increased returns to farmers should come entirely out of the federal Treasury. It should come as a surprise to no one that there was a minority, a partial minority, opinion put forward by the Liberal member of the committee. His suggestion was simply that Government make payments directly to the farmers out of the federal Treasury. I am not surprised at that because, after all, deficits are nothing new to members of that Party. Deficit-financing was, and appears to remain, that Party's answer to everything. It seems to think that we should mortgage tomorrow to pay for
Committee Reports
today's programs. It says: never pay today what you can refinance tomorrow, and continue to roll the debt over and let someone else worry about it down the road.
The idea of making a deficiency or a subsidy payment directly to farmers out of the federal Treasury is an interesting one. It is easy and it is simple. I said earlier that it is rather seductive and dangerous because the federal deficit today, with the combined excesses of the past, comes to some $235 billion. The carrying charges on that deficit are in the area of $25 billion to $28 billion per year. Thus, one out of every four government expenditure dollars goes to service that debt, and one out of every three revenue dollars gathered by Government today pays interest on the debt. In fact, without the interest charges on the national debt the Government is very close to balancing the books, even in the face of historically low wheat and oil prices.
To his credit the member of the New Democratic Party who sat on the committee recognized that the consumer is part of the equation and ought to bear some of the impact of the effect of the world grain subsidy wars on Canadian producers along with the farmers and the Government. He recognizes that the problem with borrowing to finance all that is required to assist agriculture at this time puts the Government and indeed all of us in a classic catch-22 situation. Each time the Government resorts to the Treasury or borrows more money, upward pressure is put on interest rates. Interest rates, of course, are the price of money and reflect the supply and demand. They tend to move upwards when there is demand for it. If the Government borrows more, there is a crowding out effect and the competition for money increases, with the result that interest rates rise.
I should point out that back in 1984, Canadian farm debt in the aggregate was estimated to be some $21 billion. No doubt that figure has increased since that time. A 1 per cent increase in the interest rate on a debt of $21 billion plus comes to something in the order of $210 million. That sum is roughly equivalent to the amount of benefit to grain producers that an increase in the domestic wheat price of $3 would provide. In other words, a 1 per cent interest rate increase across the board would pretty well cancel out the benefit of an increase in the domestic wheat price from $7 to $10. Clearly it is unacceptable to resort to the Treasury as the entire answer.
The second alternative with which the committee was faced was to increase the domestic wheat price. Increasing the domestic wheat price is, I believe, a vote of confidence in the concept of two-price wheat, a concept which has been in effect in Canada for many years. The basic premise of it is that a price range is set within which domestic wheat can fluctuate up and down depending on conditions and circumstances. When world wheat prices are high, the domestic wheat price would be fixed at or near the bottom of the range so as to protect Canadian consumers against unusually high prices. Conversely, when world wheat prices are low, as it appears

June 19, 1986
Committee Reports
they will be for the foreseeable future and particularly for the crop year commencing August 1, the domestic wheat price should be fixed at or near the top of the range so as to provide some measure of assistance to Candian grain farmers who face unreasonable foreign subsidization.
While the negative impact on prices of wheat-based products was observed by the committee, the advantages to an increase in the domestic wheat price far outweigh any down side. The two-price wheat system is well known, is established and has worked reasonably well in the past. Second, it produces a transfer of funds to the wheat producer at the lowest possible administrative cost. Third, and very important, it provides flexibility to respond within a stated range to changes in world price conditions. The domestic wheat price can move up and down in inverse relationship to the world price. Fourth, as I mentioned earlier, the announcement made by the Prime Minister gives some hope to producers that the Government is cognizant of the problems they face and that within the limitations inherent in the two-price wheat system, some adjustments can be made.
The third alternative facing the committee was to consider replacing the two-price wheat policy. The committee listened to many points of view and heard some suggestions that the Government should fund the entire program. Some suggested that the Government should get rid of the two-price system altogether leaving us with just one price, the world price. The committee heard suggestions that the Government should consider some sort of levy or tariff at the point of sale, and indeed, at first blush, the suggestion of a tariff or levy on agricultural-based products at or near the point of retail sale does have some appeal. Such a system could theoretically minimize the impact of a wheat price increase being built on over and over again in the food-chain between the farm gate and the supermarket shelf.
How nice it would be if it were possible to capture a levy at a point of sale and return it intact to the farm sector. Unfortunately, as has been pointed out earlier in debate, there are a number of pitfalls which attach to the food levy concept. First and most compelling is the notion that this would be construed as a food tax. I think that notion has been found to be distasteful to the majority of Canadians. Second, and this is an important factor as well, the administrative mechanism required to put forward such a program promises to be exremely expensive. We were advised informally that such a mechanism might cost something in the order of $100 million to establish and run. Clearly Canada does not need another bureaucracy which could so dissipate the benefits of any such levy or tariff.
At present, there is certainly no mechanism in place nor any intention to impose a system whereby a tariff or levy could be imposed on the sale of agricultural-based products at or near retail sale. Such a mechanism would require a considerable lead time to establish and certainly would not be available to respond to the problems of today even if the philosophy or principle behind it found favour with the committee and the
House. The symbolism involved in a levy on food is, I think, such that it would certainly require all-Party consent before such a levy would be put forward. Clearly I think there is no suggestion of that and indeed no enthusiasm from any source concerning it.
We have been considering all of the alternatives and emphasizing the one constant theme that we heard throughout the hearings, which is the inadequate return to wheat producers. This theme was repeated time and time again, not only by farmers and farm groups but also by consumers, processors and other wheat users. It became obvious that the committee must find a way to lend assistance to this sector of Canadian agriculture. The subsidization of the Common Agricultural Policy of the European Economic Community is now being met head-on by the Americans who are determined to retain their traditional market shares. In fact, the Americans are entering into markets which had been traditionally Canadian. It is essential that all means of enhancing and improving returns to wheat producers be retained. Therefore, the committee made a series of recommendations.
The first recommendation was that the current two-price wheat policy be retained. The second was that the domestic wheat price be increased to $10 per bushel. This, incidentally, should manifest itself, if adopted, in an increase of approximately 25 cents per bushel across the Canadian Wheat Board area and something in excess of that in the Ontario area. It was also suggested that if this is implemented, it should certainly be reviewed and monitored from time to time. This is important because it should be understood that this recommendation is of an interim nature. If Canadian grain farmers were receiving $6 per bushel today, there would be no need for a domestic wheat price increase or for a domestic wheat policy because all involved in the process would be most pleased.
The fourth recommendation, and the important one put forward by the committee, was that the Government give consideration to a deficiency or stabilization payment for the forthcoming crop year. In dealing with this recommendation, it is important to note that some farmers may be beyond help. Rightly or wrongly, some farmers bought assets at the wrong time and may have outbid others for land and cannot now expect the prudent ones to save them.
This recommendation is not a cure-all and it is certainly not a panacea. The Government cannot and indeed ought not try to devise schemes to prevent all farm failures. Some farmers will fail as will some small business people and some professionals. The Government is not in a position to guarantee everyone's success or to put forward a freedom from failure policy.
Considering the compelling situation facing Canadian agriculture, I believe that the Government must make a reasoned and measured response in the face of these difficult world conditions to assist Canadian agriculture to survive over the next several years and to give efficient young operators a fighting chance to succeed in the future.

June 19, 1986
In my travels I detected that producers do not expect miracles. They do not expect Government to cure all their problems, problems which they recognize are not the making of the Government or the making of Canadian agriculture. I also detect that producers would be satisfied if their returns for the forthcoming crop year, for the 1986-87 crop year, were equal to what they will receive for the current crop year, the 1985-86 crop year. That would be my personal suggestion to the House.
In saying this, I recognize that at this time it is simply too soon to determine what support would be necessary because world wheat stocks, while they are large, could certainly disappear in a hurry, and that has happened in the past. To make an early panic payment for political expediency would not serve the country well. If in fact part way through the next crop year prices have materially improved, the need for Government involvement would certainly be lessened or in fact could disappear.
The point is that we are talking about a crop year which has not yet begun, the crop year that will begin on August 1. In the meantime, farmers can rest assured that the Government understands the problems of agriculture and is indeed sympathetic to them.
Concerns were raised with the committee about possible change in production patterns motivated by the increase in the domestic wheat price. Therefore, the committee suggests that the Minister of State for Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) try to ensure that the two-price wheat policy continue to reflect historic market share. In other words, if 95 per cent has previously gone to the Canadian Wheat Board area and 5 per cent elsewhere, then the benefits should continue to be so allocated regardless of any changes in regional volume.
I note, Mr. Speaker, that you are signalling that my time is almost up. I should like to conclude by saying that the establishment of the two-price wheat committee is consistent with a long line of initiatives which have been put forward by the Government, by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) and by the Minister of State for Canadian Wheat Board. It must be noted that the recommendation to increase the price of wheat domestically from $7 to $10 per bushel is a partial response. If conditions continue and unfold as projected, clearly that increase in domestic wheat price, if it comes about, will not be enough. If these future forecasts prove correct, clearly more action is necessary-consequently, the fourth recommendation concerning the deficiency or stabilization payment. Indeed, we have commitments from the involved Ministers that the Government will continue its support of agriculture.
The report of the Special Committee on the Pricing of Domestic Wheat means many things. Should Government act on it, it will mean more for the farmer, as I mentioned earlier. It will mean marginally higher prices to the consumers of wheat-based products. I trust they will recognize that this is an
Committee Reports
interim and urgent measure designed as a response to the crisis in which Canadian farmers find themselves. The report noted that the pricing regime intended to prevent undue increases to consumers. There was a stated intention to prevent regional dislocation. Also the report recognizes that the two-price wheat system is not an entire answer but rather part of the solution, and certainly the Government Treasury is not the entire answer. As well, the report emphasizes the importance of trade negotiations both through GATT and through the pursuit of an international grain agreement.
Finally, I should like to say that I think it represents a bit of a triumph in terms of parliamentary process and parliamentary reform, in that a Private Member can put forward a motion with some expectation that something may come of it. In terms of that process, we have been able to follow a Private Member's Bill which in turn has manifested itself in a special committee, which in turn has been constituted to travel the country and has been in a position to formulate a report to the House. That process indicates that Private Members can have meaningful input, input which can and does influence government policy.
I see that my time has come to an end. I thank the House for providing me with that time.
